the sentences from my note on Tocqueville … — ECS, pp. 25–33. Schmitt wrote this text while interned.
E. R. Curtius — Ernst Robert Curtius (1886–1956), Romance-language scholar. He had known Schmitt since at least 1914, and the two had also been friends.
In 1922 Curtius supervised the doctorate of Schmitt’s lover Kathleen Murray; see Tb 1921–24.
The relationship later broke down because Curtius mistakenly believed Schmitt had been responsible for an intrigue directed against him.
See Tb 1912–15, p. 212; also Rolf Nagel, ed., “Briefe von Ernst Robert Curtius an Carl Schmitt 1921–22,” in Archiv für das Studium der Neueren Sprachen und Literaturen 133, 1981, pp. 1–15.
oboedientia fecit hinc imperantem — “Obedience is what makes the ruler here.” Attributed to Spinoza.
Peterheinrich Kirchhoff — (1886–1973), businessman and politician from Plettenberg, member of the Bundestag, and friend of Schmitt.
Josef Wagner — (1899–1945), like Schmitt a Prussian state councillor. He served as Gauleiter in Westphalia and Silesia but came into conflict with the Nazi regime because of his Catholicism.
In 1941 he was stripped of all his offices and, after the 20 July plot, arrested. Shortly before the end of the war he died under circumstances that remain unclear.
“the verbal sophisms of poor Karl Max” — “Karl” was added later. This is obviously a blending of Karl Schmidt—see above, note to p. 74—and Max Stirner.
Ed. Zeller — Schmitt is referring to Eduard Zeller, Geschichte der deutschen Philosophie seit Leibniz, 2nd ed., Munich 1873.
G. Nebel — Schmitt owned Gerhard Nebel, Von den Elementen. Essays, Wuppertal 1947, RW 265 no. 22280.
“your essay” — H. Schelsky, “Der Pfahlbau. Kann die deutsche Demokratie funktionieren? – Wir fragen einen amerikanischen Soziologen [= J. Schumpeter],” in Volk und Zeit 2, 1947, pp. 337–342.
“to encounter the spirit of Joseph Schumpeter again after so long” — Schmitt was in contact with the Austrian economist Joseph Schumpeter (1883–1950) when both taught at the University of Bonn.
Two letters and one postcard from Schumpeter dating from 1926–1927 survive among Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 nos. 14793–14795.
Sauermann — Probably Heinz Sauermann (1905–1981), sociologist and economist.
Ernst Lewalter — E. Lewalter, Francis Bacon. Ein Leben zwischen Tat und Gedanke, Berlin 1939.
Ernst Trendelenburg — (1882–1945), jurist and politician, Reich Economics Minister from 1930 to 1932. See Zeitschrift für Politik 25, 1935, p. 297; VA, p. 7.
G. Ferrero — Guglielmo Ferrero (1871–1942), Italian liberal historian, sociologist, and writer.
Schmitt is referring to the following passage:

“Everyone here is an optimist and would be ashamed to expect nothing good from the future. American optimism! It is a wonderful dawn in the gray history of the world, this American optimism. And yet Europe sometimes dares to laugh at this optimism as childishness.”
G. Ferrero, Zwischen zwei Welten. Ein Erlebnisroman, vol. 1, Berlin/Vienna/Leipzig [1925], p. 150.

“I cannot refrain here from saying that optimism—unless it is merely the thoughtless chatter of people whose flat foreheads contain nothing but words—appears to me not only as an absurd way of thinking, but as a truly wicked one: a bitter mockery of the nameless sufferings of humanity.”
Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation, in Werke in zehn Bänden (Zurich edition), vol. 2, I/2, Zurich 1977, pp. 407–408.
supplet naturam — “It supplies what nature lacks” or “it completes nature.” A formula found both in Roman law and in scholastic theology.
Le Corps Politique — Thomas Hobbes, Le Corps Politiqve Ov Les Elements de la Loy Morale & Civile. Avec Des Reflections Sur la Loy de Nature, sur les Serments …, Leiden, Jean & Daniel Elsevier, 1653.
Günther Krauss — (1911–1989), pupil of Schmitt, who supervised his doctorate in 1935.

Oraison funèbre — Bossuet’s funeral oration for Louis II de Bourbon, Prince de Condé: Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, Oraison Funebre De Tres-Haut Et Tres-Puissant Prince Louis De Bourbon Prince De Condé, Premier Prince Du Sang. Prononcée dans l’Eglise de Nostre-Dame de Paris le 10. jour de Mars 1687, Paris 1687.
Budde-style — Eugen Budde (1901–1984), jurist, diplomat, and author of numerous memoranda.
In 1947 he published Gibt es noch eine deutsche Außenpolitik? Betrachtungen zur Politik und Diplomatie eines geschlagenen Staates.
Below — Georg von Below (1858–1927), historian of constitutional and economic history, who engaged in extensive methodological debates with Max Weber.

Günther Krauss’s dissertation in Berlin in 1934 — The dissertation of the Catholic Krauss, supervised at the University of Berlin by C. Schmitt and the Protestant Rudolf Smend, dates not from 1934 but from 1935:
Günther Krauss, Der Rechtsbegriff des Rechts. Eine Untersuchung des positivistischen Rechtsbegriffs im besonderen Hinblick auf das rechtswissenschaftliche Denken Rudolph Sohms, Hamburg 1935.
Schmitt’s annotated copy survives among his papers, RW 265 no. 28435. See also RW 265 nos. 21240 and 21495.
“Both Smend and Brinkmann wrote to me with tactless forgiveness” — See BW Smend, pp. 117 ff. On Brinkmann, see above, note to p. 74.
“for the old—that is, the young—Theodor Haecker” — Schmitt valued the polemical Haecker of the First World War period, but not the later Haecker. See the entry for 2 July 1948.
To Mrs. Jünger — See BW GJ, pp. 104–105.
OdF card — Opfer des Faschismus, “Victim of Fascism.” The Berlin committee of that name issued cards granting their holders privileged access to supplies.
Dr. Epstein — Kurt Epstein, who as a Jew had suffered under Nazi persecution, headed the compensation department of the Hessian Ministry for Political Liberation as a senior government official.
He was also president of the regional association of Jewish communities in Hesse.
Niekisch letters — Ernst Niekisch (1889–1967), national-revolutionary political writer who had initially sympathized with Schmitt.
In 1933 Niekisch reviewed Schmitt’s The Concept of the Political in Widerstand 8, 1933, pp. 369–375.
In connection with the review, he wrote to Schmitt on 25 September 1933:

“Your essay The Concept of the Political is giving me a great deal to think about. You know how highly I regard it. If I were to review it briefly, I would praise it without reservation and would not even hint at the problem I see in the background. Certain thoughts have occurred to me, however, which I would first like to discuss with you. They concern a certain polarity: ‘enemy — opponent.’ Is there perhaps a contrast here between a Mediterranean and a Nordic understanding?”
After 1945 Niekisch sharply criticized Schmitt in several publications for his decision to side with National Socialism.
The fact that Niekisch also used insinuations in doing so placed a strain on Schmitt’s relationship with Ernst and Gretha Jünger, who remained friends with Niekisch.
See below, p. 377: “Do not forget that because of your friendship with Ernst Jünger.”
On the relationship between Schmitt and Niekisch, see BW EJ, passim, and BW Mohler, pp. 164 ff. and 254 ff.
Causa victrix diis placuit, sed victa Catoni — “The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato.” Pharsalia I, 128.
Cato the Younger (95–46 BC) was famous for his uprightness and strict sense of justice. After Caesar’s victory in the civil war, he committed suicide.

Vitoria’s seven legal titles — Francisco de Vitoria, Relecciones teológicas. Edición crítica, con facsimil de códices y ediciones príncipes, variantes, versión castellana, notas e introducción, edited by Luis G. Alonso Getino, vols. 1–3, Madrid 1933–1935.
Schmitt worked from this edition, RW 265 no. 25201.
On Schmitt’s engagement with Vitoria, see Nomos, pp. 69 ff.
A sentence by the early-modern jurist Alberico Gentili which Schmitt often quoted.
“Be silent, theologians, when dealing with matters outside your field.”
“The removal of jurists from an international law treated theologically found its first clear expression here.”

the disputation between Las Casas and Sepúlveda — In Valladolid in 1550 the Dominican Bartolomé de Las Casas and the secular priest and humanist Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda debated the legitimacy of the Spanish conquest and the enslavement of the Indigenous peoples of South America.
James Brown Scott — (1866–1943), American scholar of international law. On Schmitt’s dispute with him, see Angriffskrieg.
Jackson — Robert H. Jackson (1892–1954), chief United States prosecutor at the Nuremberg war-crimes trials.
the Savigny-Hegel polarity — In 1958 Schmitt said that one of the great omissions of his life was his failure to publish a study of the relationship between Savigny and Hegel. VA, p. 428.
events in Prague — In 1948 the Czechoslovak president Edvard Beneš was forced from office, and the country became communist under Soviet pressure.

In a letter to Michael Freund dated 1 November 1950, Schmitt insisted that these events were comparable with what had happened in Germany in the spring of 1933, and that in Legality and Legitimacy he had worked out “with complete clarity” their model situation for modern democracy.
Beneš — Edvard Beneš (1884–1948), president of Czechoslovakia; in exile from 1940 to 1945.
Hácha’s role — Emil Hácha (1872–1945), president of Czechoslovakia.
After Slovakia declared independence, Hácha was summoned to Berlin on 14 March 1939 for negotiations with Hitler.

Hitler, Göring, and others put him under enormous pressure, including threats to bomb Czech cities. The pressure was so intense—Hitler later used the expression “to Hácha-ize” someone for this kind of treatment—that Hácha collapsed.
In the early hours of 15 March, after recovering from the collapse, he agreed to the occupation of his country by German troops.
Already in very poor health, he then remained as a figurehead at the head of the German Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia.
He died under circumstances that remain unclear.
